raw_evidence.content: Frosted tips — bleached or colored hair ends over a darker base — became a defining visual marker of late-90s/early-2000s teen pop, worn by Justin Timberlake of NSYNC, Brian Littrell of Backstreet Boys, Lance Bass, and many imitators. Hair stylists at the time tied the look to the choreographed-pop aesthetic: dark roots gave on-camera contrast under stage lighting, and the bleach-tip effect aged 16-year-old members up for music videos without crossing into adult-rock territory. The look has since become a costume-only marker of that exact moment in pop history, which means any spike in 'frosted_tips=yes' in the data should map cleanly to 1996-2002.

Reading 1980-2018 boyband data without this scaffolding flattens three different genres into one chart line.

def era_pct(field, value, members):

def era_pct(field, value, members):
    """Among members in this era, what % match field == value (or token in field)."""
    if not members:
        return 0.0
    n = sum(1 for r in members if value in (r[field] or "").split(","))
    return n / len(members) * 100

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Pudding's Internet Boy Band Database (Nov 2018)
raw_evidence.content: The dataset comes from The Pudding's November 2018 visual essay 'Internet Boy Band Database', written by Amber Thomas with motion graphics by Malik Yusuf and design/development by Russell Samora. The team began with a candidate list pulled from five sources (BuzzFeed, Billboard, Teen Vogue, the Wikipedia 'American boy bands' category, and Ranker), then filtered to 55 acts that (a) had at least one song chart on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100 between 1980 and 2018 and (b) had a YouTube version of that highest-charting (and earliest, in case of ties) song available. From those 55 music videos, more than 40 volunteers manually annotated 234 individual band members for hair, clothing, accessories, instruments, skin tone, height, and date of birth — each member double-coded with a third reviewer breaking ties. This is therefore not a survey of every boy band ever; it is a careful field guide to what charting boy bands actually looked like on screen.

raw_evidence.label: Definition trap: 'classifying boy bands is not an exact science'
raw_evidence.content: Pudding's editors acknowledge the genre is fuzzy. The dataset's filtering rule — Billboard Hot 100 + a charting music video + a manageable number of male singers — picks up vocal R&B groups (Boyz II Men, Jodeci, Blackstreet, Shai), rap-adjacent acts (Bell Biv DeVoe, Mindless Behavior), and global imports (Westlife, Take That, Aventura, BTS) alongside the prototypical American 'prefab' acts. That is a feature, not a bug: it lets us see how a category that pop culture treats as a single thing — 'boy band' — actually contains four or five overlapping micro-genres whose look and music differ markedly. Any finding from this data should be read as 'across the kinds of male vocal groups that crossed over to U.S. pop charts', not as a universal claim about all boy bands.

The team began with a candidate list pulled from five sources (BuzzFeed, Billboard, Teen Vogue, the Wikipedia 'American boy bands' category, and Ranker), then filtered to 55 acts that (a) had at least one song chart on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100 between 1980 and 2018 and (b) had a YouTube version of that highest-charting (and earliest, in case of ties) song available. From those 55 music videos, more than 40 volunteers manually annotated 234 individual band members for hair, clothing, accessories, instruments, skin tone, height, and date of birth — each member double-coded with a third reviewer breaking ties. This is therefore not a survey of every boy band ever; it is a careful field guide to what charting boy bands actually looked like on screen.

raw_evidence.content: The 55 charting bands cluster into a handful of clear lineages. New Edition spawns Bell Biv DeVoe (literal members of NE). The Lou Pearlman empire produces Backstreet Boys, NSYNC, O-Town, and LFO. British/Irish imports (Take That, BBMak, Westlife, 5ive, Brother Beyond) form the late-1990s Anglo wave. Disney/tween-TV produces Jonas Brothers, Big Time Rush, and Mindless Behavior. Imports outside the Anglo world include BTS (K-pop), Aventura (Bachata/Latin), Menudo (Puerto Rico), and Son by Four. Reality-TV pop produces One Direction, The Wanted, and 5 Seconds of Summer. Reading the dataset as one chart line obscures these branches; reading them as a tree explains why hair, skin tone, and dance speed turn over so sharply era-by-era.

    n = len(members)
    if not n:
        continue
    suit = sum(1 for r in members if "suit jacket" in (r["top_style"] or ""))
    print(f"  {ds}: suit-jacket-tops {suit}/{n} ({suit/n*100:.0f}%)")

# --- ana_24: average band size by era ---
print("\n=== ana_24 ===")
band_size = Counter(r["band"] for r in boys)
for e in ERAS:
    bands_in_era = [b for b in bands if era_label(int(b["highest_pos_date"][:4])) == e]
    if not bands_in_era:
        continue
    sizes = [band_size[b["band"]] for b in bands_in_era]
    print(f"  {e}: bands={len(sizes)}, mean members={sum(sizes)/len(sizes):.2f}")

Source: the-pudding/data — boybands README (https://github.com/the-pudding/data/tree/master/boybands) Facts: Reviewers were instructed to describe members 'when all members were featured together in the same shot'; Each band's highest-ranking music video on YouTube was the only source examined

raw_evidence.label: Why a music-video sample matters
raw_evidence.content: Pudding intentionally coded the highest-charting single's music video, not press photos or candid shots. That matters because music videos are the most stage-managed view of a boy band: stylists, choreographers, and label image consultants control every visible detail. So the frequencies in the dataset are not a neutral sample of how members looked off duty — they are a sample of what the industry decided viewers should see. When 110 of 234 members are in dress pants and 91 are wearing 'navy blue' or 'black' bottoms, that is a deliberate visual codification, not a statement about real-life fashion of young men in the 1990s.

raw_evidence.label: 47.4% wear black, white, or navy on top AND bottom
raw_evidence.content: The unofficial uniform of the music video is monochrome: 111 of 234 members (47.4%) wear shirts and bottoms drawn entirely from black, white, or navy blue. The single most common combination is white shirt + black bottoms (33 members, 14.1%), followed by black shirt + navy blue (30, 12.8%), all-black (26, 11.1%), and white + navy blue (22, 9.4%). Across 23 shirt colors and 10 bottom colors — over 200 possible combos — five of them account for over half the members.
raw_evidence.code:
with open(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "boys.csv"), encoding="utf-8") as f:
    boys = list(csv.DictReader(f))

# --- ana_27: shirt color + bottom color (top combos) ---
print("=== ana_27 ===")
combo = Counter((r["shirt_color"], r["bottom_color"]) for r in boys)
print(f"Total members: {len(boys)}, distinct shirt-bottom combos: {len(combo)}")
print("Top 10 shirt+bottom combos:")
for (s, b), n in combo.most_common(10):
    print(f"  {s!r:18s} + {b!r:14s}  {n:3d}  ({n/len(boys)*100:.1f}%)")

# --- ana_28: monochrome members ---
print("\n=== ana_28 ===")
mono_black = sum(1 for r in boys if r["shirt_color"] == "black" and r["bottom_color"] == "black")
mono_white = sum(1 for r in boys if r["shirt_color"] == "white" and r["bottom_color"] == "black")  # white tee navy/black
white_navy = sum(1 for r in boys if r["shirt_color"] == "white" and r["bottom_color"] == "navy blue")
black_navy = sum(1 for r in boys if r["shirt_color"] == "black" and r["bottom_color"] == "navy blue")
white_black = sum(1 for r in boys if r["shirt_color"] == "white" and r["bottom_color"] == "black")
print(f"  all black (shirt+bottom): {mono_black} ({mono_black/len(boys)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  white shirt + navy bottom: {white_navy} ({white_navy/len(boys)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"  white shirt + black bottom: {white_black} ({white_black/len(boys)*100:.1f}%)")

sentences.summary: det_05: Why frosted tips became a 1999 signal. Source: Boy band — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_band) Facts: Late-1990s boy bands developed identifiable hair and wardrobe trends, including frosted tips Source: NSYNC vs. Backstreet Boys — Rolling Stone (https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/n-sync-vs-backstreet-boys-reme) Facts: NSYNC and Backstreet Boys members were widely associated with frosted/dyed hair tips circa 1998-2000

raw_evidence.label: Why frosted tips became a 1999 signal
raw_evidence.content: Frosted tips — bleached or colored hair ends over a darker base — became a defining visual marker of late-90s/early-2000s teen pop, worn by Justin Timberlake of NSYNC, Brian Littrell of Backstreet Boys, Lance Bass, and many imitators. Hair stylists at the time tied the look to the choreographed-pop aesthetic: dark roots gave on-camera contrast under stage lighting, and the bleach-tip effect aged 16-year-old members up for music videos without crossing into adult-rock territory. The look has since become a costume-only marker of that exact moment in pop history, which means any spike in 'frosted_tips=yes' in the data should map cleanly to 1996-2002.

raw_evidence.label: Why frosted tips became a 1999 signal
raw_evidence.content: Frosted tips — bleached or colored hair ends over a darker base — became a defining visual marker of late-90s/early-2000s teen pop, worn by Justin Timberlake of NSYNC, Brian Littrell of Backstreet Boys, Lance Bass, and many imitators. Hair stylists at the time tied the look to the choreographed-pop aesthetic: dark roots gave on-camera contrast under stage lighting, and the bleach-tip effect aged 16-year-old members up for music videos without crossing into adult-rock territory. The look has since become a costume-only marker of that exact moment in pop history, which means any spike in 'frosted_tips=yes' in the data should map cleanly to 1996-2002.

raw_evidence.label: Skin-tone composition flips by era
raw_evidence.content: Skin-tone composition turns over almost completely across the 35 years. In the early 1990s, only 14% of members are coded light; 77% are medium-dark or dark — the New Edition / Boyz II Men / Jodeci R&B-pop wave. Five years later in the late 1990s, light-skin share jumps to 33%; in the early 2000s it reaches 61%, and medium-dark-or-dark falls to 22% — the prefab Backstreet/NSYNC peak. By the early 2010s, light-skin members are 59% and medium-dark-or-dark members are 5% — the One Direction / 5SOS / The Wanted slice is overwhelmingly white. The boy band charts visibly desegregated for one decade and then re-segregated.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: U.S. ethnic and skin-tone composition for context
raw_evidence.content: U.S. Census 2010-2018 figures show that the country's male population aged 15-24 — roughly the age range of charting boy band members — was approximately 60% non-Hispanic white, 14% Black, 18% Hispanic, and 6% Asian. The Pudding skin-tone coding ('light' / 'medium-light' / 'medium' / 'medium-dark' / 'dark') does not map perfectly to those census categories, but it lets us check whether the people who sang on Top 40 radio looked like the kids who were buying the records. If, say, 'dark' members account for 16% of boy band members but Black men are 14% of the relevant U.S. population, the boy band ecosystem broadly mirrored its audience; large gaps in either direction would be a story.

raw_evidence.label: Background: what 'boy band' actually means
raw_evidence.content: Boy bands are usually defined as vocal groups of young male singers — typically four or five — built for a teenage audience, with harmony and choreographed performance over instrumental virtuosity. Britannica and Wikipedia trace the modern term to the 1980s, when MTV-era groups like Menudo, New Edition, and New Kids on the Block established the template. The format reached commercial peak in the late 1990s and early 2000s with the Backstreet Boys and NSYNC, who together sold more than 200 million records, and was reinterpreted in the 2010s by One Direction (Western pop) and BTS (K-pop), the latter becoming the first non-English boy band to top the Billboard 200. Crucially, the genre is built on visible identity: each member usually plays a distinct 'type' (the cute one, the bad boy, the dancer, the singer), and the music video — not the album — is the primary product.

raw_evidence.label: The era waves: 1989-1991 R&B teen swing, 1996-2001 pop boom, 2010s Tumblr/K-pop
raw_evidence.content: Music historians generally divide the boy band era into three waves. Wave one (1988-1992) is dominated by New Edition's R&B descendants — Bell Biv DeVoe, Boyz II Men, Color Me Badd, Hi-Five, Shai, Jodeci — with formal suits, soulful slow jams, and a New Jack Swing edge. Wave two (1996-2001) is the prefabricated pop explosion engineered by managers like Lou Pearlman (Backstreet Boys, NSYNC, O-Town, LFO) plus the British/Irish import wave (Take That, Westlife, 5ive). Wave three (2010-present) breaks the formula: One Direction emerges from a TV show in matching streetwear and skinny jeans, and BTS exports a fundamentally different aesthetic — South Korean idol training, choreography, and visual concepts — into the American Top 40. Reading 1980-2018 boyband data without this scaffolding flattens three different genres into one chart line.

raw_evidence.label: Background: what 'boy band' actually means
raw_evidence.content: Boy bands are usually defined as vocal groups of young male singers — typically four or five — built for a teenage audience, with harmony and choreographed performance over instrumental virtuosity. Britannica and Wikipedia trace the modern term to the 1980s, when MTV-era groups like Menudo, New Edition, and New Kids on the Block established the template. The format reached commercial peak in the late 1990s and early 2000s with the Backstreet Boys and NSYNC, who together sold more than 200 million records, and was reinterpreted in the 2010s by One Direction (Western pop) and BTS (K-pop), the latter becoming the first non-English boy band to top the Billboard 200. Crucially, the genre is built on visible identity: each member usually plays a distinct 'type' (the cute one, the bad boy, the dancer, the singer), and the music video — not the album — is the primary product.

raw_evidence.label: Skin-tone composition flips by era
raw_evidence.content: Skin-tone composition turns over almost completely across the 35 years. In the early 1990s, only 14% of members are coded light; 77% are medium-dark or dark — the New Edition / Boyz II Men / Jodeci R&B-pop wave. Five years later in the late 1990s, light-skin share jumps to 33%; in the early 2000s it reaches 61%, and medium-dark-or-dark falls to 22% — the prefab Backstreet/NSYNC peak. By the early 2010s, light-skin members are 59% and medium-dark-or-dark members are 5% — the One Direction / 5SOS / The Wanted slice is overwhelmingly white. The boy band charts visibly desegregated for one decade and then re-segregated.
